verses.1: Al-Mizan takes wa al-fajr primarily as dawn in an unrestricted sense, while allowing the dawn of the tenth of Dhū al-Ḥijjah, the Day of Sacrifice, as possible. It records several other proposals—including dawns of Muḥarram or Friday, the Night of Gathering, the Morning Prayer, the whole day, and springs’ eruption—as weak possibilities.
verses.2: Al-Mizan apparently identifies the ten nights with the first ten days of Dhū al-Ḥijjah, and says their indefinite form conveys glorification; it records the first or last ten of Ramadan, the first ten of Muḥarram, and ten nights of worship as alternatives. An authorial note says the wāw marks an oath in these clauses. An editor’s note explains that the Night of Gathering was originally proposed for (89:4), and its association with dawn was added later by mistake.
verses.3: Al-Mizan defines shafʿ as pairing or attaching like things, and takes al-shafʿ and al-watr most appropriately as the Day of Tarwiyah, the eighth of Dhū al-Ḥijjah, and the Day of ʿArafah, the ninth, if the preceding oaths concern that period. It records narration-based and other readings as the optional night prayers, all prayers, the Day of Sacrifice and ʿArafah, humanity and God, even and odd numbers, all beings, Adam and Eve, all days and nights versus the Resurrection, al-Ṣafā and al-Marwah versus the Kaʿbah, ʿĀd’s days and nights, and paradise’s and hell’s gates. It notes the philosophical reading in which God is the absolute, simple Necessary Being and other beings are compound contingents, but judges most of the many proposed interpretations unfounded impositions on the verse.
verses.4: Al-Mizan says sary means the passing and ending of night, so the oath concerns night as it departs, comparable to (74:33). Because al-layl is generic, it takes the reference as the last part of all nights. It finds the proposal of the Muzdalifah night problematic, particularly if the ten nights are the first ten of Dhū al-Ḥijjah.
verses.5: Al-Mizan reads the rhetorical question as confirmation that the preceding vows are sufficient for one with ḥijr, that is, ʿaql (intellect, reason, wit), to distinguish truth from falsehood. A divine oath confirms a statement’s certainty and the significance of what is sworn by. Its omitted complement is inferred from the chapter’s warnings of punishment, reward for souls at peace, and the testing character of bestowed or withheld blessings; omitting it heightens the warning and glad tidings.
verses.6: Al-Mizan identifies this as the former ʿĀd (53:50), whose prophet was Hūd and whose home was al-Aḥqāf, the sand-dunes (46:21). It notes that their recurring Qur’anic account was discussed under 11:50-60.
verses.7: Al-Mizan takes Iram to be a city of ʿĀd, with ʿimād meaning pillars that uphold a structure: apparently a prosperous, unmatched city of lofty palaces and colonnades. It says only brief Qur’anic accounts remain: ʿĀd came after Noah’s people, lived in al-Aḥqāf, were powerful and physically sturdy, and possessed an advanced, fertile civilization. It rejects as far from the text readings that make Iram their forefather and the pillars their political power, or that make them nomads living in tents. It identifies the famous Garden of Iram accounts as mythical reports from Wahb b. Munabbih and Kaʿb al-Aḥbār.

verses.9: Al-Mizan derives jābū from jawb, meaning cutting, carving, or cleaving, and reads it as hewing mountain houses, as in (26:149).
verses.10: Al-Mizan identifies this Pharaoh as Moses’ contemporary. It reports narrations that call him possessor of pegs because he tortured victims by pegging their limbs to the ground or wood, supported by his threat to crucify the believing magicians on palm trunks (20:71).
verses.11: Al-Mizan says ʿĀd, Thamūd, and Pharaoh are the peoples who rebelled and spread corruption. It explains fa-ṣabba as pouring down and the scourge as a metaphor for recurrent, frequent, indescribably excruciating punishment poured upon each transgressing people; the indefinite punishment intensifies that meaning.

verses.14: Al-Mizan explains la-bil-mirṣād through the metaphor of an ambush: God watches and records His servants’ deeds and, when they transgress and spread corruption, seizes them with the severest punishment. The wording your Lord also indicates that this divine custom, shown with earlier peoples, applies equally to the Prophet’s community.
verses.15: Al-Mizan says human beings mistake bestowed worldly bounty for proof of their honor and lasting entitlement, and withheld provision for divine disgrace; in fact, God tests them by both. Al-insān denotes humankind according to its natural disposition, and ibtilāʾ means examination. Bestowal is an apparent or initial honor meant to prompt gratitude and service, but people can turn it into a curse through transgression. Their claim to be honored expresses this inclination rather than necessarily spoken words; my Lord reflects the fiṭrah that recognizes God’s Lordship even where idolaters and atheists do not acknowledge it.
verses.16: Al-Mizan reads tightened provision as another divine test, not proof of dishonor. The repeated testing in both plenty and want shows that good and ill are trials (21:35); bounty is an honor only if one does not turn it into misfortune. It rejects equating worldly enjoyment with honor, holding that real honor is nearness to God through faith and righteous deeds, equally available to rich and poor.
verses.17: Al-Mizan says kallā and bal refute the equation of wealth with honor and poverty with disgrace: both bestowal and withholding are tests of servitude and obedience. Bal intensifies rebuke through direct address and supplies evidence of wealth without virtue: failing to honor orphans by depriving them of inheritance, failing to urge mutual charity for the needy, consuming inheritance indiscriminately through lamman, and loving wealth abundantly through jamman. Taḥāḍḍūna means urging one another to feed the needy; the human fiṭrah itself judges such wealth dishonorable.

verses.21: Al-Mizan says the leveling of the earth, dakk, on the Resurrection refutes the belief that worldly wealth and poverty are final values: they are tests through which people should prepare their eternal life, but those absorbed in them will regret too late. God’s coming is mutashābih and must be read through muḥkam verses such as (42:11), which establish His incomparability and the removal of veils and means of recourse on that day. It reports narrations interpreting the coming as His amr, supported by (2:210) and (16:33), while allowing a figurative attribution. Hell’s being brought near probably means its unveiling; awakening then cannot help because the day is for retribution, not repentance and action.

verses.24: Al-Mizan takes my life in both proposed senses—the life here or one’s real life—as the life of the Hereafter, the true Life (29:64). Sending ahead for it means performing righteous deeds beforehand. The regret comes when people awaken on the Resurrection but can no longer benefit from that awakening.
verses.25: Al-Mizan takes He in both clauses as God, whose punishment and binding on that day exceed anything any creature can inflict, intensifying the warning. It also records the passive recitation, lā yuʿadhdhabu and lā yūthaqu, in which the human being is punished and confined as no one else is.

verses.27: Al-Mizan contrasts the soul at peace with the worldly, transgressing, corrupt, ungrateful group. Such a soul is at peace with its Lord and pleased with what pleases Him, sees itself as a servant without independent command over benefit or harm, treats this world as temporary, and knows abundance and deprivation as tests. It therefore remains established in servitude, neither proud and corrupt in plenty nor ungrateful and unbelieving in want.
verses.28: Al-Mizan says this address accompanies the soul from death through resurrection until its settlement in paradise, not only after reckoning. Being pleased with God comprises acceptance of His takwīnī decrees, without resentment at what occurs, and His tashrīʿī decrees, without disturbance by temptation to sin. Because God is displeased by violating servitude, a servant who keeps its path and is pleased with Him is in turn pleasing to Him.
verses.29: Al-Mizan treats this as the consequence of returning to God: the soul at peace has reached the station of servitude. Peace with the Lord means abandoning any claim to independence, recognizing Him as absolute owner of one’s essence, attributes, and acts, and desiring only what He wills in both creation and legislation. Entering among His servants confirms this perfection of servitude.
verses.30: Al-Mizan says this fixes the soul’s abode. God’s direct attribution, My paradise, unique in the Qur’an, signifies a special honor and glorification of the servant’s rank.
